LUREX: Lunar Radiation Environment Explorer
MAE 342 · Spacecraft Design · Team of 16
Propulsion · Launch Vehicle
Presenting the LUREX Propulsion & Launch Vehicle poster with the team
Propulsion module CAD: hydrazine and MON-3 tank layout

Led propulsion and launch vehicle systems engineering for a two-satellite lunar mission (MiLO and LiLO) designed to characterize the lunar radiation environment from low and mid lunar orbit. Built the formal requirements, ΔV budget, and thruster trade study that drove the propulsion architecture. Led a propulsion and launch vehicle subteam of four.

Selected a shared hydrazine tank feeding both a MON-3 main engine and eight monopropellant RCS thrusters to minimize failure points, then sized propellant load, tank volume, and wet mass against ESPA Grande secondary-payload constraints. Also contributed to the power subsystem's solar array sizing and battery energy budget.

Main engineLE144, Isp 328s
PropellantHydrazine / MON-3
RCS thrusters8× monoprop, ~1N
MiLO wet mass251.3 kg
LiLO wet mass228.4 kg

Alternative Propellants for Hall Effect Thrusters
MAE 426 · Research Presentation · Team of 5
Electric Propulsion
Published HET performance data: xenon vs. solid iodine propellant
HET with inclined inward plume divergence

A research presentation synthesizing published studies on solid iodine as a low-cost alternative to xenon and argon for Hall effect thrusters, framed as a response to SpaceX's switch to argon in the Starlink V2 Mini. Iodine's atomic mass and ionization energy closely track xenon's, while its solid storage at 3x the density of pressurized xenon and ~$30/kg cost (versus thousands per kilogram for xenon) make it attractive for constellation-scale deployment.

Separately reviewed published findings on how inward-inclined magnetic topology and combined radial propellant injection reduce plume divergence and improve ionization uniformity, both of which compound favorably with iodine's heavier-than-argon atomic mass. Closed with a forward-looking case for in-situ propellants (lunar/Martian magnesium, water ice) that would eliminate Earth-based resupply entirely.

Iodine ideal thrust257 mN
Anode efficiency65%
Storage density3× pressurized Xe
Propellant cost−98.6% vs. Xe
Plume divergence42.3° → 35.3°

Cislunar Infrastructure Policy Study
Beeson Group, Princeton University · IAC 2026
Policy · Research
IAC 2026 paper: governmental and commercial perspectives on cislunar infrastructure

Co-authored an exploratory study on incentive-based policy adoption strategies for cislunar orbital sustainability, conducted with Arjun Chhabra under Prof. Ryne Beeson. The work characterizes which shared cislunar services (space situational awareness, communication relays, and similar infrastructure) could be made conditional on operators meeting non-binding debris-mitigation standards.

Solicited and analyzed perspectives from a cross-section of commercial, governmental, and academic spacecraft operators, alongside the regulators who would oversee access to these services, to map where incentive-based compliance is viable and where it breaks down.

VenueIAF E6 Symposium
Congress77th IAC, 2026
Paper ID109145
Co-authorsA. Chhabra, Prof. R. Beeson

Shepard: Mars Sojourner Recovery Trajectory
MAE 341 · Spaceflight Dynamics · STK Astrogator
Orbital Mechanics
Full interplanetary trajectory: STK Astrogator output

Designed a full interplanetary mission concept in STK to recover NASA's long-dormant Sojourner rover from Mars and return it to Earth. Built Earth-to-Mars and Mars-to-Earth transfer arcs with Lambert solvers, a Mars parking orbit inclined to repeatedly overfly the Ares Vallis landing site, and a 16-month hold in Mars orbit timed to the next return launch window.

Worked through real STK constraints along the way (propagator accuracy versus runtime, differential-corrector convergence for orbit insertion and inclination changes) that mirror the trade-offs mission designers face when building long-duration interplanetary sequences.

Mission duration32 months
Total ΔV22.6 km/s
Transfer legs221 days each
Mars hold16 months
Landing siteGulf of Mexico

Megatron: Autonomous Search & Rescue Robot
Mechanical Design Course · Team Lead, Team of 10
Mechanical Systems
Completed chassis: large-wheel drivetrain and arm
Cleated wheel detail: the wall-breaching mechanism

Owned the chassis and drivetrain for a large-wheel autonomous robot built to navigate a simulated disaster course and deliver a medical kit to a trapped victim. The signature mechanism (oversized cleated wheels that double as the wall-breaching method) came from a free-body analysis of the torque needed to climb a 6-inch breach wall, which set the wheel radius and motor sizing.

Coordinated integration across the mechanical, electrical, and software teams through final delivery; the robot was the only one in the course to complete the full course autonomously.

Weight38.6 lb (50 lb max)
Course time~1:00 (5:00 max)
Top speed~2.8 mph
Wall breach success80%
Budget recycled33%
